content: Laetoli is a significant archaeological site located in Tanzania, dating back to the Plio-Pleistocene epoch. It is renowned for its exceptionally well-preserved hominid footprints, which were embedded in volcanic ash at a location known as Site G. This site is situated approximately 45 kilometers south of Olduvai Gorge. Since the late 1990s, Professor Terry Harrison, a physical anthropologist from New York University, has been conducting ongoing research at Laetoli. In 1978, a team led by Mary Leakey, Richard Hay, and Tim White discovered a series of hominid fossil footprints at Laetoli. These footprints were preserved in a layer of fine volcanic ash, which originated from an eruption of the Sadiman Volcano, located about 20 kilometers away. A light rain subsequently cemented the 15-centimeter-thick ash layer into a hardened tuff, preserving the footprints without damaging them. Over time, additional ash deposits covered the prints, protecting them further. The footprints were made by three individuals, with one walking in the tracks of another, which made the original tracks more challenging to identify. The alignment of the tracks suggests they may have been created by a group, but there is no definitive evidence to support the common interpretation of a nuclear family visiting a waterhole together. The footprints provide critical evidence that these hominids habitually walked upright, as there are no impressions of knuckles, which would indicate quadrupedal movement. The feet lacked the opposable big toe characteristic of apes and instead displayed an arch, a feature typical of modern human feet. The stride and spacing of the footprints suggest the hominids were moving at a leisurely pace. In addition to the hominid footprints, the site contains tracks of approximately 20 other animal species, including hyenas, wild cats (Machairodont), baboons, wild boars, giraffes, gazelles, rhinoceroses, various antelope species, hipparion (an extinct horse), buffalo, elephants of the extinct Deinotherium genus, hares, and birds. Raindrop impressions are also visible in the ash layer. The minimal overlap of footprints indicates that the tracks were quickly covered by subsequent ash deposits. Many of these animal species are also represented by skeletal remains found in the area. The first researcher to explore Laetoli for fossil remains was the German anthropologist Ludwig Kohl-Larsen, who, in 1934, discovered a jawbone attributed to Australopithecus afarensis. To date, the remains of 13 hominids have been uncovered at Laetoli, primarily consisting of mandibles and teeth. These remains show similarities to the famous female skeleton Lucy from Hadar, Ethiopia. Most scholars classify these fossils as Australopithecus afarensis, although some argue for a closer resemblance to the genus Homo and prefer to label them as Homo sp. indet. A relatively complete skull discovered at Ngaloba in 1976 has been dated to approximately 120,000 to 100,000 years ago. This skull exhibits modern anatomical features, including a cranial capacity of about 1200 cm³, but it retains a notably low forehead. No artifacts have been found in the vicinity of the Laetoli site. For further reading, notable references include: Mary D. Leakey and J.M. Harris (eds.), Laetoli: A Pliocene Site in Northern Tanzania (Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1987). ISBN 0-19-854441-3. Richard L. Hay and Mary D. Leakey, Fossil Footprints of Laetoli, Scientific American, February 1982, pp. 50-57.
